meta.subject: history
meta.description: US History facts: American Revolution, Civil War, Constitution, Civil Rights, presidents, westward expansion, industrialization, WWI/WWII, immigration, Native Americans

facts.statement: The Declaration of Independence was adopted on July 4, 1776
The U.S. Constitution was signed on September 17, 1787, and ratified in 1788
The American Civil War lasted from 1861 to 1865
The United States entered World War I in 1917 and World War II in 1941 (after Pearl Harbor, December 7, 1941)
The Civil Rights Act of 1964 outlawed discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, or national origin
The first Moon landing occurred on July 20, 1969, with astronauts Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin
The Emancipation Proclamation was issued by Abraham Lincoln on January 1, 1863, declaring slaves in Confederate states free
The 19th Amendment, ratified in 1920, granted women the right to vote
The Louisiana Purchase in 1803 doubled the size of the United States, buying land from France for about $15 million
The War of 1812 between the United States and Great Britain lasted from 1812 to 1815
The Great Depression began with the stock market crash on October 29, 1929 (Black Tuesday) and lasted until about 1939
The September 11, 2001 terrorist attacks destroyed the World Trade Center in New York City and killed nearly 3,000 people

common_errors.wrong: the Declaration of Independence was signed on July 4, 1776
common_errors.correct: July 4, 1776 is when the Declaration was adopted (approved) by Congress. Most delegates signed it on August 2, 1776.

common_errors.wrong: the Civil War was only about slavery
common_errors.correct: While slavery was the central issue, the Civil War also involved states' rights, economic differences, and political power struggles between North and South.

common_errors.wrong: the Emancipation Proclamation freed all slaves
common_errors.correct: It only applied to slaves in Confederate states. Slavery was not fully abolished until the 13th Amendment was ratified in 1865.

common_errors.wrong: the Great Depression was caused only by the stock market crash
common_errors.correct: The stock market crash was a trigger, but underlying causes included overproduction, bank failures, high tariffs, and unequal wealth distribution.

facts.statement: George Washington was the first President of the United States, serving from 1789 to 1797
Abraham Lincoln was the 16th president, who led the nation through the Civil War and abolished slavery
Thomas Jefferson was the 3rd president and primary author of the Declaration of Independence
Franklin D. Roosevelt served the most terms of any president (4 terms, 1933-1945), leading through the Great Depression and most of World War II
The 22nd Amendment (ratified 1951) limits presidents to two terms in office
Theodore Roosevelt (26th president) was known for conservation, trust-busting, and building the Panama Canal
John F. Kennedy was the 35th president, assassinated on November 22, 1963, in Dallas, Texas
Andrew Jackson, the 7th president, signed the Indian Removal Act of 1830, which led to the Trail of Tears
Dwight D. Eisenhower, the 34th president, was Supreme Allied Commander in World War II before becoming president
Barack Obama became the first African American President of the United States in 2009
James Madison is called the Father of the Constitution because he played a key role in drafting the document and the Bill of Rights
Lyndon B. Johnson became president after Kennedy's assassination and signed the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965

common_errors.wrong: Benjamin Franklin was a president
common_errors.correct: Benjamin Franklin was never president. He was a Founding Father, diplomat, inventor, and signer of the Declaration of Independence.

common_errors.wrong: Abraham Lincoln freed the slaves immediately upon becoming president
common_errors.correct: Lincoln became president in 1861. The Emancipation Proclamation was issued in 1863, and the 13th Amendment abolished slavery in 1865.

common_errors.wrong: George Washington had wooden teeth
common_errors.correct: Washington's dentures were made of various materials including ivory, lead, human teeth, and animal teeth, but not wood.

common_errors.wrong: the president can make laws on their own
common_errors.correct: The president can sign or veto bills passed by Congress and issue executive orders, but only Congress can pass legislation.

facts.statement: The Bill of Rights consists of the first 10 amendments to the Constitution, ratified in 1791
The 1st Amendment protects freedom of speech, religion, press, assembly, and petition
The 13th Amendment (1865) abolished slavery throughout the United States
The 14th Amendment (1868) granted citizenship to all persons born in the United States and guaranteed equal protection under the law
The 15th Amendment (1870) prohibited denying the right to vote based on race
The 19th Amendment (1920) guaranteed women's right to vote
The 26th Amendment (1971) lowered the voting age from 21 to 18
There are currently 27 amendments to the U.S. Constitution
The 2nd Amendment protects the right to keep and bear arms in connection with a well-regulated militia
The 4th Amendment protects against unreasonable searches and seizures and requires warrants to be based on probable cause
The 5th Amendment protects against self-incrimination and double jeopardy, and guarantees due process of law
The 18th Amendment (1919) prohibited the manufacture and sale of alcohol (Prohibition), and the 21st Amendment (1933) repealed it

common_errors.wrong: the 1st Amendment gives unlimited free speech
common_errors.correct: The 1st Amendment does not protect all speech. Exceptions include threats, incitement to imminent violence, defamation, and obscenity.

common_errors.wrong: the Bill of Rights was part of the original Constitution
common_errors.correct: The Bill of Rights was added as amendments in 1791, four years after the Constitution was signed in 1787.

common_errors.wrong: the 2nd Amendment was about hunting rights
common_errors.correct: The 2nd Amendment addresses the right to bear arms in the context of a well-regulated militia. Its exact scope continues to be interpreted by courts.

common_errors.wrong: the 5th Amendment only applies in criminal trials
common_errors.correct: The 5th Amendment also applies outside of trials; it includes protections like due process and the prohibition against taking private property without just compensation.

facts.statement: Marbury v. Madison (1803) established the principle of judicial review, giving the Supreme Court the power to declare laws unconstitutional
Brown v. Board of Education (1954) declared racial segregation in public schools unconstitutional, overturning Plessy v. Ferguson
Plessy v. Ferguson (1896) upheld 'separate but equal' racial segregation, which stood until Brown v. Board of Education
Miranda v. Arizona (1966) established that arrested persons must be informed of their rights (Miranda rights) before questioning
Gideon v. Wainwright (1963) ruled that the 6th Amendment guarantees the right to a lawyer for defendants who cannot afford one
The Supreme Court has 9 justices who are appointed by the President and confirmed by the Senate for life terms
Tinker v. Des Moines (1969) ruled that students do not lose their First Amendment rights at school, as long as expression does not cause substantial disruption
Dred Scott v. Sandford (1857) ruled that African Americans were not citizens and had no standing in court, a decision later overturned by the 14th Amendment

common_errors.wrong: the Supreme Court can make new laws
common_errors.correct: The Supreme Court interprets laws and the Constitution. It can strike down laws as unconstitutional but cannot create new legislation. That power belongs to Congress.

common_errors.wrong: Brown v. Board immediately ended school segregation
common_errors.correct: The ruling ordered desegregation but did not set a timeline. Many schools remained segregated for years, and enforcement required further legal and political action.

common_errors.wrong: Supreme Court justices are elected by the public
common_errors.correct: Supreme Court justices are nominated by the President and confirmed by the Senate. They are not elected by voters.

facts.statement: The 13 original colonies declared independence from Great Britain in 1776
The Boston Tea Party (1773) was a protest against British taxation without representation, where colonists dumped tea into Boston Harbor
The battles of Lexington and Concord in April 1775 were the first military engagements of the American Revolution
The phrase 'no taxation without representation' expressed colonists' anger at being taxed by Parliament without having elected representatives there
The Continental Army, led by George Washington, defeated the British with help from France, which provided soldiers, ships, and supplies
The Treaty of Paris (1783) officially ended the American Revolution and recognized American independence
The Stamp Act (1765) taxed printed materials in the colonies and was one of the earliest sources of colonial resentment toward Britain
The Boston Massacre (1770) was a confrontation in which British soldiers killed five colonists, fueling anti-British sentiment
The Articles of Confederation were the first governing document of the United States (1781-1789), replaced by the Constitution because the central government was too weak

common_errors.wrong: Paul Revere rode alone shouting 'the British are coming'
common_errors.correct: Revere was one of several riders (including William Dawes and Samuel Prescott), and he likely said 'the Regulars are coming' since colonists were also British subjects.

common_errors.wrong: all colonists supported independence from Britain
common_errors.correct: Colonists were divided into Patriots (supported independence), Loyalists (supported Britain), and many who remained neutral.

common_errors.wrong: America won the Revolution without any foreign help
common_errors.correct: France provided crucial military and financial support. Spain and the Netherlands also helped. The French navy was decisive at the Battle of Yorktown.

common_errors.wrong: the Boston Tea Party was about the price of tea being too high
common_errors.correct: The protest was about the principle of taxation without representation, not the price of tea itself. The Tea Act actually lowered the price of tea.

facts.statement: Manifest Destiny was the 19th-century belief that the United States was destined to expand across the North American continent
The Lewis and Clark Expedition (1804-1806) explored the western territory acquired in the Louisiana Purchase, guided in part by Sacagawea
The California Gold Rush began in 1848 when gold was discovered at Sutter's Mill, attracting hundreds of thousands of settlers
The Homestead Act of 1862 gave 160 acres of public land to settlers who farmed it for five years
The Trail of Tears (1838) was the forced relocation of Cherokee and other Native American nations from their homelands to Indian Territory (present-day Oklahoma), resulting in thousands of deaths
The transcontinental railroad was completed in 1869 at Promontory Summit, Utah, connecting the East and West coasts by rail
The Oregon Trail was a major overland route used by settlers in the 1840s-1860s to travel from Missouri to the Pacific Northwest
The Mexican-American War (1846-1848) ended with the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, which gave the U.S. California, Nevada, Utah, and parts of several other states

common_errors.wrong: the American West was empty before settlers arrived
common_errors.correct: Millions of Native Americans had lived across the West for thousands of years before European-American expansion.

common_errors.wrong: all Native Americans were nomadic
common_errors.correct: Many Native American groups were settled farmers (Pueblo, Cherokee, Iroquois) or lived in permanent villages. Lifestyles varied greatly among hundreds of distinct nations.

common_errors.wrong: the transcontinental railroad was built entirely by American-born workers
common_errors.correct: Chinese immigrants made up a large portion of the workforce on the western section (Central Pacific), and Irish immigrants built much of the eastern section (Union Pacific).

common_errors.wrong: Sacagawea led the Lewis and Clark expedition
common_errors.correct: Sacagawea served as an interpreter and guide but did not lead the expedition. Meriwether Lewis and William Clark were the leaders.

facts.statement: The Civil Rights Movement of the 1950s-1960s fought to end racial segregation and discrimination against African Americans
Rosa Parks refused to give up her bus seat to a white passenger in Montgomery, Alabama, in 1955, sparking the Montgomery Bus Boycott
Martin Luther King Jr. delivered the 'I Have a Dream' speech during the March on Washington on August 28, 1963
Jim Crow laws were state and local laws in the South that enforced racial segregation from the 1870s through the 1960s
The Voting Rights Act of 1965 prohibited racial discrimination in voting, including literacy tests and other barriers
The Little Rock Nine were nine African American students who integrated Central High School in Little Rock, Arkansas, in 1957, protected by federal troops
Freedom Riders were civil rights activists who rode interstate buses in 1961 to challenge segregation in bus terminals across the South
The NAACP (National Association for the Advancement of Colored People), founded in 1909, was a major organization in the fight for civil rights
Cesar Chavez and Dolores Huerta co-founded the National Farm Workers Association to fight for the rights of migrant farmworkers
Thurgood Marshall argued the Brown v. Board of Education case and later became the first African American Supreme Court Justice in 1967

common_errors.wrong: Rosa Parks refused to give up her seat because she was tired
common_errors.correct: Parks later said she was not physically tired but 'tired of giving in.' Her refusal was a deliberate act of civil disobedience.

common_errors.wrong: Martin Luther King Jr. single-handedly led the civil rights movement
common_errors.correct: The movement involved thousands of leaders and organizations including the NAACP, SCLC, SNCC, and many unnamed activists.

common_errors.wrong: the civil rights movement only benefited African Americans
common_errors.correct: Civil rights legislation benefited all minorities, women, and other groups facing discrimination. The movement inspired other rights movements worldwide.

common_errors.wrong: racism ended when the Civil Rights Act was passed
common_errors.correct: The Civil Rights Act was a major legal milestone, but racial discrimination and inequality continued in various forms after 1964.

facts.statement: The Industrial Revolution transformed the United States from an agricultural to an industrial economy in the late 1800s
Andrew Carnegie built a massive steel empire and later became one of the greatest philanthropists, funding libraries across America
John D. Rockefeller founded Standard Oil and became one of the wealthiest Americans in history
The Gilded Age (roughly 1870s-1900) was a period of rapid economic growth but also extreme inequality, corruption, and poor working conditions
Labor unions formed to fight for better wages, shorter hours, and safer working conditions for factory workers
Thomas Edison's laboratory in Menlo Park produced inventions including the practical incandescent light bulb and the phonograph
The Progressive Era (1890s-1920s) was a period of reform addressing problems caused by industrialization, including child labor, unsafe food, and corruption
Millions of immigrants arrived at Ellis Island in New York Harbor between 1892 and 1954, seeking opportunity in industrial America

common_errors.wrong: Edison invented the light bulb
common_errors.correct: Edison improved the light bulb and made it practical for widespread use. Many inventors contributed to its development, including Humphry Davy and Joseph Swan.

common_errors.wrong: child labor was always illegal in the United States
common_errors.correct: Child labor was common in factories and mines during the 1800s. Federal child labor laws were not effectively enforced until the Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938.

common_errors.wrong: the Gilded Age only benefited the rich
common_errors.correct: While inequality was extreme, industrialization also created new jobs, lowered the cost of goods, and built infrastructure that benefited many Americans over time.

facts.statement: The United States is often called a nation of immigrants because people from all over the world have settled here throughout its history
Ellis Island in New York processed over 12 million immigrants between 1892 and 1954, mostly from Europe
Angel Island in San Francisco Bay processed immigrants from Asia, particularly Chinese immigrants, between 1910 and 1940
The Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882 was the first federal law to restrict immigration based on nationality, barring Chinese laborers from entering the US
During World War II, approximately 120,000 Japanese Americans were forcibly relocated to internment camps by Executive Order 9066
The Immigration and Nationality Act of 1965 eliminated national-origin quotas and opened immigration from Asia, Africa, and Latin America
The Statue of Liberty, a gift from France dedicated in 1886, became a symbol of welcome for immigrants arriving in New York
The Great Migration (1910-1970) saw approximately 6 million African Americans move from the rural South to cities in the North, Midwest, and West

common_errors.wrong: all immigrants to America came through Ellis Island
common_errors.correct: Ellis Island primarily processed European immigrants. Asian immigrants often came through Angel Island, and many others arrived through other ports or overland.

common_errors.wrong: Japanese internment during WWII was justified by actual espionage
common_errors.correct: No evidence of widespread Japanese American espionage was ever found. The internment is now widely recognized as a grave injustice driven by wartime fear and racism.

common_errors.wrong: the Statue of Liberty was built in the United States
common_errors.correct: The Statue of Liberty was designed by French sculptor Frederic Auguste Bartholdi and built in France. It was shipped to America in pieces and assembled on Bedloe's Island.

common_errors.wrong: immigrants always assimilated quickly and easily
common_errors.correct: Immigrants often faced discrimination, language barriers, and economic hardship. Assimilation happened over generations, not overnight.
